questionText: Series: 64,81,100,121,... Which number NOT in series?
hints: Look at what kind of numbers are in the series. Each one comes from multiplying a number by itself.
64 is 8 × 8 and 81 is 9 × 9. Test each choice to see whether it is a number multiplied by itself.
Here is a similar one: the series 1, 4, 9, 16 holds square numbers. 49 belongs, because 7 × 7 = 49. 50 does not belong, because it falls between 7 × 7 = 49 and 8 × 8 = 64.

stepByStep.text: The series is 8 × 8, 9 × 9, 10 × 10, 11 × 11. These are square numbers.
169 is 13 × 13, 225 is 15 × 15 and 289 is 17 × 17. They all belong.
13 × 13 = 169 and 14 × 14 = 196. No whole number multiplied by itself gives a number between these two.
176 lies between 169 and 196. So 176 is not in the series.

misconceptions.A: 169 is 13 × 13, so it is in the series. Look for the number that is not a number times itself.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 176 falls between 13 × 13 and 14 × 14, so it is not a square number.
misconceptions.C: 225 is 15 × 15, so it is in the series. Look for the number that is not a number times itself.
misconceptions.D: 289 is 17 × 17, so it is in the series. Look for the number that is not a number times itself.

questionText: Sum of series 1,3,5,7,...,27?
hints: These are the odd numbers in order, starting from 1. Sums of odd numbers starting from 1 make a special pattern.
Try small cases first, such as 1 + 3 and 1 + 3 + 5. Then count how many odd numbers there are from 1 to 27.
Here is a similar one: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 has 5 odd numbers and adds up to 25. That is 5 × 5. So the sum of the first 5 odd numbers is (5)².

stepByStep.text: Look at small cases. 1 + 3 = 4, which is 2 × 2. And 1 + 3 + 5 = 9, which is 3 × 3. The sum is always the count of odd numbers multiplied by itself.
Count the odd numbers from 1 to 27. Add 1 to 27 and halve it.
There are 14 odd numbers, so the sum is 14 × 14.
So the sum is (14)².

misconceptions.A: Count the odd numbers again. 27 is the 14th odd number, not the 13th.
misconceptions.B: Yes! There are 14 odd numbers from 1 to 27, so the sum is 14 × 14.
misconceptions.C: Count how many odd numbers there are: (27 + 1) ÷ 2. The sum is that count multiplied by itself.
misconceptions.D: The sum depends on how many odd numbers there are, not on how big the last one is. Count them: (27 + 1) ÷ 2.

questionText: The pattern 4, 9, 14, 19, ... goes up by 5 each time and ends at 99. How many of its numbers are even?
hints: First see which numbers in the pattern are even and which are odd. Then count only the ones you need, taking care with the first and the last.
The pattern goes even, odd, even, odd: 4, 9, 14, 19. The even ones end in 4. Find where they start and where they stop.
Similar problem: 3, 8, 13, 18, ..., 48. The even numbers are 8, 18, 28, 38, 48, which is 5 numbers.

stepByStep.text: Adding 5 changes even to odd and odd to even, so the numbers take turns: 4 is even, 9 is odd, 14 is even, and so on.
The even numbers are the ones ending in 4: 4, 14, 24, ..., 94.
From 4 to 94 in jumps of 10 there are 9 jumps, so there are 10 numbers.
10 of the numbers in the pattern are even.

misconceptions.A: 20 is how many numbers the whole pattern has. Only every second one is even, starting with 4.
misconceptions.B: This is (99 − 4) ÷ 5, the number of jumps in the whole pattern. Look only at the even numbers: 4, 14, 24, and so on.
misconceptions.C: From 4 to 94 there are 9 jumps of 10, but that makes 10 numbers, because both ends are counted.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The even ones are 4, 14, 24, 34, 44, 54, 64, 74, 84 and 94, which is 10 numbers.

questionText: A number pattern goes up and down like this: 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3, 4, ... What is the 100th number in the pattern?
hints: Find the block of numbers that repeats again and again. Be careful about exactly where one block ends and the next begins.

stepByStep.text: The repeating block is 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2. The next 1 starts a new block, so a block has 6 numbers, not 7.
100 ÷ 6 is 16 with remainder 4, so 16 full blocks use up 96 numbers.
The 100th number is the 4th number of the next block: 1, 2, 3, 4.
The 100th number in the pattern is 4.

misconceptions.A: This uses 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2, 1 as the block, with 7 numbers. The last 1 is really the start of the next block, so a block has 6 numbers.
misconceptions.B: Great job! The block 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2 has 6 numbers; 96 numbers fill 16 blocks, and the 100th is the 4th number of the next block.
misconceptions.C: The block of 6 is the right idea. After 96 numbers, count 4 more places: 1, 2, 3, 4. This lands one place too far.
misconceptions.D: The 100th number does not start or finish a block. Find how many numbers are left after the full blocks.

questionText: What is the value of 20 − 19 + 18 − 17 + 16 − 15 + ... + 2 − 1? The numbers go down one at a time from 20 to 1, and the signs take turns.
hints: Do not work from left to right through all twenty numbers. Look for small groups that are easy to work out.

misconceptions.B: The numbers do not cancel completely. Each pair, such as 20 − 19, leaves 1.
misconceptions.C: Excellent! Each pair such as 20 − 19 is worth 1, and 20 numbers make 10 pairs.
misconceptions.D: 1 is the value of one pair, such as 20 − 19. Count how many pairs there are.

questionText: Farid arranges dots in rows to make a triangle. The 1st row has 1 dot, the 2nd row has 2 dots, the 3rd row has 3 dots, and so on. He has 60 dots and makes as many complete rows as he can. How many dots are left over?
hints: Keep a running total of the dots used as each new row is added, and stop before the total goes past the dots he has.

5 dots are left over.

misconceptions.B: 10 is the number of complete rows he makes. The question asks how many dots are left over after those rows.
misconceptions.C: 6 is 66 − 60, the extra dots he would need to finish an 11th row. The question asks how many dots he has left after the 10th row.
misconceptions.D: No dots would be left only if 60 were one of the running totals 1, 3, 6, 10 and so on. Keep adding rows and see whether you land exactly on 60.

questionText: Find the rule in this pattern: 2, 6, 4, 12, 10, 30, 28, ... What is the 10th number in the pattern?

The 10th is 82 × 3.
The 10th number in the pattern is 246.

misconceptions.B: 84 is the 8th number, the next one after 28. Carry on two more steps to reach the 10th.
misconceptions.C: 82 is the 9th number. One more step, times 3, gives the 10th.

questionText: Pattern A is 5, 9, 13, 17, ... and goes up by 4 each time. Pattern B is 2, 9, 16, 23, ... and goes up by 7 each time. The number 9 is in both patterns. What is the next number that is in both patterns?

misconceptions.B: 65 is in both patterns, but one shared number comes before it. Look for the first one after 9.
misconceptions.C: 33 is in pattern A, but pattern B goes 23, 30, 37 and misses it. The number must be in both.
misconceptions.D: Excellent! Both patterns meet again 28 after 9, and 9 + 28 = 37.

questionText: A number pattern goes up by the same amount each time. Its 5th number is 23 and its 8th number is 35. What is the 1st number of the pattern?

Now count how many digits each number has: 7, 6, then a gap, then 4 and 3. The count goes down by 1 each time, so the missing number has 5 digits.
The digit 5 written 5 times is 55555. The missing term is 55555.

misconceptions.A: Excellent thinking! The digit drops by 2 to 5 and the length drops by 1 to five digits, which gives 55555.
misconceptions.B: The digit 5 is right, but this number has six 5s, the same length as 777777. Each number is one digit shorter than the one before.
misconceptions.C: The digit 5 is right, but this number has only four 5s, the same length as 3333. The lengths go 7, 6, then the gap, then 4 and 3.
misconceptions.D: The length is right, but check the digit. The digits go 9, 7, then the gap, then 3 and 1, going down by 2 each time.

questionText: What is the next term in the sequence: 416, 525, 636, 749, ______
hints: Look at the jumps between the terms. If the jumps are not all the same, look for a pattern in the jumps themselves.
Subtract to find the three jumps: from 416 to 525, from 525 to 636 and from 636 to 749. See how much each jump grows by.
Here is a similar one: 200, 305, 412, 521. The jumps are 105, 107 and 109, going up by 2. The next jump is 111, so the next term is 521 + 111 = 632.

stepByStep.text: The jumps are not all the same, which is the thing to spot here. They go 109, 111, 113, growing by 2 each time, so the next jump is 115.
Add 115 to the last term to get 864.

You can check another way. The first digits go 4, 5, 6, 7, and the last two digits are 16, 25, 36 and 49, which are 4 × 4, 5 × 5, 6 × 6 and 7 × 7. Next comes 8 followed by 8 × 8 = 64, so the next term is 864.

misconceptions.A: 961 is a much bigger jump than the others. The jumps are 109, 111 and 113, so the next jump is only a little bigger.
misconceptions.B: 884 is 749 + 135. The jumps grow by just 2 each time, so the next jump is 115.
misconceptions.C: Excellent thinking! The jumps are 109, 111, 113 and then 115, and 749 + 115 = 864.
misconceptions.D: 881 is 749 + 132. The jumps are 109, 111 and 113, so add 115 to 749.

questionText: Find the number in place of the question mark: 2, 6, 12, 20, ?, 42, 56
hints: Look at the jumps between the numbers and see how the jumps themselves change. The numbers after the gap can help you check.
Work out the jumps from 2 to 6, from 6 to 12 and from 12 to 20. See how much each jump grows by.
Here is a similar one: 1, 5, 11, 19, a gap, then 41. The jumps are 4, 6 and 8, going up by 2. The next jump is 10, so the missing number is 19 + 10 = 29. As a check, 29 + 12 = 41.

stepByStep.text: Find the jumps: 6 − 2 = 4, 12 − 6 = 6 and 20 − 12 = 8.
The jumps go up by 2 each time, so the next jump is 10.
Add 10 to 20 to get 30.
Check with the numbers that follow: 30 + 12 = 42 and 42 + 14 = 56, so the pattern holds. The missing number is 30.

misconceptions.A: 28 is 20 + 8, using the last jump again. The jumps grow by 2 each time.
misconceptions.B: 32 is 20 + 12. Then the jump from 32 to 42 would be only 10, so the jumps would stop growing.
misconceptions.C: 24 is 20 + 4, using the first jump again. The jumps are 4, 6 and 8, so the next one is bigger than 8.
misconceptions.D: Well done! The jumps are 4, 6, 8 and then 10, and 20 + 10 = 30.

questionText: What is the next number in the sequence: 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, ______
hints: These numbers do not grow by a steady jump. Try making each one by multiplying a small number by itself more than once.
Start with 8, which is 2 × 2 × 2. Now see whether 27 and 64 can be made the same way using 3 and 4.
Here is a similar pattern: 1, 4, 9, 16. These are 1 × 1, 2 × 2, 3 × 3 and 4 × 4, each counting number multiplied by itself. The next one is 5 × 5 = 25.

stepByStep.text: Each number is a counting number used three times in a multiplication: 1 × 1 × 1 = 1, 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 and 3 × 3 × 3 = 27.
The pattern carries on: 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 and 5 × 5 × 5 = 125.
The next number uses 6. First 6 × 6 = 36, and then 36 × 6 = 216. The next number is 216.

misconceptions.A: 225 is 15 × 15. This pattern uses each counting number three times, so try 6 × 6 × 6.
misconceptions.B: You got it! The numbers are 1 × 1 × 1, 2 × 2 × 2 and so on, and 6 × 6 × 6 = 216.
misconceptions.C: 169 is 13 × 13. Here each number is used three times, like 5 × 5 × 5 = 125.
misconceptions.D: 185 is 125 + 60. The jumps here are not steady, so look at 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 and 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 instead.

hints: Look at the jumps between the terms and see what kind of numbers the jumps are. You need to carry the pattern on for two more terms.
Work out the four jumps from 53 up to 83. Ask yourself which times table these jumps belong to.
Here is a similar one: 10, 12, 16, 22, 30. The jumps are 2, 4, 6 and 8, the multiples of 2 in order. The next two jumps are 10 and 12, so the next terms are 30 + 10 = 40 and 40 + 12 = 52.

stepByStep.text: The jumps are the multiples of 3 in order, so the next two jumps are 15 and 18.
Add 15 to 83 to get the first missing term, 98.
Add 18 to 98 to get the second missing term, 116. The next two terms are 98, 116.

misconceptions.A: Great job! The jumps are 3, 6, 9, 12 and then 15 and 18, which gives 98 and 116.
misconceptions.B: 98 is right, but 128 is 98 + 30. After a jump of 15, the next jump is 18.
misconceptions.C: 107 is 83 + 24, which doubles the last jump. The jumps go up by 3 each time: 3, 6, 9, 12 and then 15.
misconceptions.D: 98 is right, but 113 uses the jump of 15 a second time. The jump after 15 is 18.

questionText: What is the missing number: 525, 438, ______, 264, 177, 90
hints: The numbers in this sequence are getting smaller. Find how much is taken away each time, using two numbers that sit next to each other.
Subtract 438 from 525 to find the drop. Check it with another pair of neighbours, such as 264 and 177.
Here is a similar one: 400, 335, a gap, 205, 140. Each number is 65 less than the one before, because 400 − 335 = 65. The missing number is 335 − 65 = 270. As a check, 270 − 65 = 205.

stepByStep.text: Find the drop from the first two numbers.
Check with other neighbours: 264 − 177 = 87 and 177 − 90 = 87. The drop is always 87.
Take 87 away from 438 to get 351.
Check that the next drop fits: 351 − 87 = 264, which matches. The missing number is 351.

misconceptions.A: 349 is 2 too few. Take 87 away from 438 carefully, then check that taking 87 away again gives 264.
misconceptions.B: Well done! Each number is 87 less than the one before, and 438 − 87 = 351.
misconceptions.C: From 324 down to 264 is a drop of only 60, but every drop in this sequence is 87. Take 87 away from 438.
misconceptions.D: 353 is 2 too many. Take 87 away from 438 carefully, then check that taking 87 away again gives 264.

questionText: Which number should replace the asterisk? 37, 39, 42, 47, 54, *, 78
hints: Look at the jumps between the numbers. They are not steady and they do not grow evenly, so ask yourself what special family of numbers they belong to.
Write down the four jumps from 37 up to 54. Think about numbers that have exactly two factors, 1 and the number itself.

Here is a similar one: 10, 12, 15, 20, 27, a gap, then 51. The jumps are 2, 3, 5 and 7, the prime numbers in order. The next prime is 11, so the missing number is 27 + 11 = 38. As a check with the prime after that, 38 + 13 = 51.

stepByStep.text: The jumps 2, 3, 5 and 7 are the prime numbers in order. They are not simply the odd numbers, because 9 is not a prime. The next two primes are 11 and 13.
Add the next prime, 11, to 54 to get 65.
Check with the prime after that: 65 + 13 = 78, which matches the last number. The missing number is 65.

misconceptions.A: 63 is 54 + 9, as if the jumps were odd numbers. The jumps 2, 3, 5 and 7 are prime numbers, and 9 is not a prime.
misconceptions.B: Excellent thinking! The jumps are the primes 2, 3, 5, 7 and then 11, and 54 + 11 = 65.
misconceptions.C: 64 is 54 + 10. Look at the jumps 2, 3, 5 and 7 again and name the family of numbers they belong to.
misconceptions.D: 67 is 54 + 13, which skips a prime. After 7 the next prime is 11, and 13 comes after that.

questionText: Find the 10th term in the sequence: 53, 60, 68, 77, ......
hints: Look at the jumps between the terms and see how the jumps themselves change. Then keep the pattern going, counting the terms carefully as you go.
Work out the three jumps from 53 up to 77. Notice that 77 is the 4th term, so decide how many more jumps you need.
Here is a similar one. Find the 7th term of 20, 23, 27, 32. The jumps are 3, 4 and 5, going up by 1. Carry on with jumps of 6, 7 and 8: 32 + 6 = 38, 38 + 7 = 45 and 45 + 8 = 53. The 7th term is 53.

stepByStep.text: Find the jumps: 60 − 53 = 7, 68 − 60 = 8 and 77 − 68 = 9. Each jump is 1 bigger than the one before.
77 is the 4th term, so six more jumps are needed to reach the 10th term. They are 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 and 15. Counting these jumps correctly is the tricky part.
The 5th term is 77 + 10 = 87, the 6th is 87 + 11 = 98 and the 7th is 98 + 12 = 110.
The 8th term is 110 + 13 = 123 and the 9th is 123 + 14 = 137.
Add the last jump, 15, to 137. The 10th term is 152.

misconceptions.A: 123 is the 8th term. Count the terms carefully and add two more jumps.
misconceptions.B: 163 is too large. Add the jumps 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 and 15 to 77 one at a time, keeping count of the term number.
misconceptions.C: Great job! Six more jumps, from 10 up to 15, take 77 up to 152, the 10th term.
misconceptions.D: 168 is the 11th term, one jump too far. Stop when you reach the 10th term.

questionText: Find the next two terms: 4, 7, 11, 18, 29, ______, ______
hints: The jumps in this sequence are not steady. Look at how each term is linked to the two terms just before it.
Add the first two terms, 4 and 7, and compare the total with the third term. Then try the same with 7 and 11.
Here is a similar one: 2, 5, 7, 12, 19. Each term is the sum of the two before it: 2 + 5 = 7, 5 + 7 = 12 and 7 + 12 = 19. The next two terms are 12 + 19 = 31 and 19 + 31 = 50.

stepByStep.text: The jumps are 3, 4, 7 and 11, which is not a steady pattern. Look instead at terms that sit next to each other.
Each term is the sum of the two terms before it: 4 + 7 = 11, 7 + 11 = 18 and 11 + 18 = 29.
Add the last two terms to get the next term, 47.
The term after that uses the two newest terms, 29 and 47, which make 76. The next two terms are 47, 76.

misconceptions.A: 47 is right, but 65 is 47 + 18, which adds an older term. Add the two newest terms, 29 and 47.
misconceptions.B: You got it! Each term is the sum of the two before it, so the next terms are 18 + 29 = 47 and 29 + 47 = 76.
misconceptions.C: 37 is 29 + 8, as if the jumps were steady. Try adding the two terms just before the gap, 18 and 29.
misconceptions.D: 47 is right. For the term after it, add 29 and 47 once more, ones first and then tens.

questionText: Find the next term in the sequence: 1/5, 2/5, 4/5, 7/5, 11/5, ______
hints: All the fractions have the same bottom number, so the pattern is in the top numbers. Find the pattern there, then write your answer in the same form as the choices.
Write down just the top numbers: 1, 2, 4, 7, 11. Work out the jump from each one to the next.

Here is a similar one: 1/4, 2/4, 4/4, 7/4. The bottom number stays 4. The top numbers 1, 2, 4, 7 jump by 1, 2 and 3, so the next jump is 4 and the next top number is 7 + 4 = 11. The next term is 11/4, which is 2 3/4.

stepByStep.text: The bottom number is always 5, so look only at the top numbers: 1, 2, 4, 7, 11.
The jumps between the top numbers are 1, 2, 3 and 4. The next jump is 5.
The next top number is 11 + 5, which is 16. So the next term is 16/5.
Change 16/5 to a mixed number. 16 divided by 5 is 3 with 1 left over, so the next term is 3 1/5.

misconceptions.A: 7/5 is already in the sequence as the fourth term. The terms keep growing, so the next one is bigger than 11/5.
misconceptions.B: 2 1/5 is the same as 11/5, the last term given. The next term has a bigger top number.
misconceptions.C: 1 4/5 is the same as 9/5, which is smaller than 11/5. The top numbers keep growing: 1, 2, 4, 7, 11.
misconceptions.D: Well done! The next top number is 11 + 5 = 16, and 16/5 is the same as 3 1/5.

questionText: Find the number in place of the asterisk: 0.25, 0.50, 1, 1.75, *, 4
hints: Look at the jumps between the numbers and see how the jumps themselves change. The last number, 4, can help you check.
Work out the jumps from 0.25 to 0.50, from 0.50 to 1 and from 1 to 1.75. See how much each jump grows by.

Here is a similar one: 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1.4, a gap, then 3.2. The jumps are 0.2, 0.4 and 0.6, growing by 0.2 each time. The next jump is 0.8, so the missing number is 1.4 + 0.8 = 2.2. As a check, 2.2 + 1 = 3.2.

stepByStep.text: The jumps grow by 0.25 each time, so the next jump is 1.
Add 1 to 1.75 to get 2.75.
Check with the next jump, which is 1.25: 2.75 + 1.25 = 4, which matches the last number. The missing number is 2.75.

misconceptions.A: 2.25 is 1.75 + 0.50, using an old jump. The jumps are 0.25, 0.50 and 0.75, so the next one is bigger.

misconceptions.D: Great job! The jumps are 0.25, 0.50, 0.75 and then 1, and 1.75 + 1 = 2.75.

questionText: What is the next term: 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, ______
hints: Look at how much is added each time to get from one number to the next. See whether it is always the same.
Subtract 3 from 7 to find the first jump. Check that the jump from 7 to 11 is the same.

Add 4 to the last term. The next term is 23.

misconceptions.A: You got it! Each term is 4 more than the one before, and 19 + 4 = 23.
misconceptions.B: 21 is 19 + 2. Check the jump between the terms: 7 − 3 is 4, not 2.
misconceptions.C: 22 is 19 + 3. The jump between the terms is 4 each time, so add 4.
misconceptions.D: 25 is 19 + 6. The jump between the terms is 4 each time, so add 4.

Compare 3 and 6, then 6 and 12. Ask yourself how many times bigger each number is than the one before.

questionText: What comes next: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ______

Work out 2 × 2, 3 × 3 and 4 × 4 and compare them with the numbers in the list.

stepByStep.text: The jumps go up by 1 each time, so the next jump is 7.
Add 7 to the last number. The next number is 28.

misconceptions.A: 25 is 21 + 4, using an old jump. The jumps are 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, so the next one is bigger than 6.
misconceptions.B: Great job! The jumps are 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and then 7, and 21 + 7 = 28.

questionText: What is the next term: 2, 5, 14, 41, ______
hints: Look at the jumps between the terms. They are not steady, so see how each jump is made from the jump before it.
Work out the three jumps: from 2 to 5, from 5 to 14 and from 14 to 41. Ask yourself how many times bigger each jump is than the last.
Here is a similar one: 1, 3, 7, 15. The jumps are 2, 4 and 8, each double the one before. The next jump is 16, so the next term is 15 + 16 = 31.

stepByStep.text: Find the jumps: 5 − 2 = 3, 14 − 5 = 9 and 41 − 14 = 27.
The jumps do not grow by adding. Each jump is 3 times the one before: 3 × 3 = 9 and 9 × 3 = 27. So the next jump is 81.
Add 81 to the last term to get 122.
You can check another way. Each term is 3 times the one before, take away 1. 41 × 3 = 123 and 123 − 1 = 122, so the next term is 122.

misconceptions.A: 50 is 41 + 9, using an old jump. The jumps 3, 9 and 27 get 3 times bigger each time.
misconceptions.B: 120 is close. Find the next jump by multiplying 27 by 3, then add it to 41.
misconceptions.C: Excellent thinking! The jumps are 3, 9, 27 and then 81, and 41 + 81 = 122.

questionText: Find the next term: 1, 2, 6, 24, 120, ______

Work out what 1 is multiplied by to give 2, then what 2 is multiplied by to give 6, then 6 to give 24. Look at those multipliers in order.
Here is a similar one: 4, 8, 24, 96. Here 4 × 2 = 8, 8 × 3 = 24 and 24 × 4 = 96. The multiplier goes up by 1 each time, so the next term is 96 × 5 = 480.

stepByStep.text: See what each term is multiplied by to get the next: 1 × 2 = 2, 2 × 3 = 6, 6 × 4 = 24 and 24 × 5 = 120.
The multiplier goes up by 1 each time: 2, 3, 4, 5. The next multiplier is 6.
Multiply the last term by 6. The next term is 720.

misconceptions.A: 360 is 120 × 3, using an old multiplier. The multipliers go 2, 3, 4, 5, so the next one is 6.
misconceptions.B: You got it! The multipliers are 2, 3, 4, 5 and then 6, and 120 × 6 = 720.
misconceptions.C: 240 is 120 × 2, using the first multiplier again. The multipliers go 2, 3, 4, 5, so the next one is 6.
misconceptions.D: 600 is 120 × 5, using the last multiplier again. The multiplier grows by 1 each time.

questionText: Find the missing number: 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, ______
hints: The jumps here are not steady. Look at how each number is linked to the two numbers just before it.
Add the first two numbers, 2 and 3, and compare the total with the third number. Then try the same with 3 and 5.
Here is a similar one: 1, 4, 5, 9, 14. Each number is the sum of the two before it: 1 + 4 = 5, 4 + 5 = 9 and 5 + 9 = 14. The next number is 9 + 14 = 23.

stepByStep.text: Each number is the sum of the two before it: 2 + 3 = 5, 3 + 5 = 8, 5 + 8 = 13 and 8 + 13 = 21.
Add the last two numbers. The missing number is 34.

misconceptions.A: Well done! Each number is the sum of the two before it, and 13 + 21 = 34.
misconceptions.B: 29 is 21 + 8, using the last jump again. Add the last two numbers of the list instead.
misconceptions.C: 26 is 21 + 5. Each number here is the sum of the two numbers before it.

questionText: Which number does NOT belong: 2, 5, 10, 17, 28, 37
hints: When one number does not fit a pattern, look at the gaps between neighbours. In a good pattern the gaps follow a rule, and the odd one out breaks it.
Find the gap between each pair of neighbours, starting with 2 and 5, then 5 and 10. Write the gaps in a row and look for the place where their rule breaks.

Here is a similar one: 3, 5, 9, 15, 25, 33. The gaps are 2, 4, 6, 10, 8. They should grow by 2 each time: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. So after 15 the number should be 15 + 8 = 23, and 23 + 10 = 33 fits. The number that does not belong is 25.

stepByStep.text: Find the gaps between neighbours: 5 − 2 = 3, 10 − 5 = 5, 17 − 10 = 7, 28 − 17 = 11 and 37 − 28 = 9.
The gaps 3, 5, 7 go up by 2 each time, so the next gaps should be 9 and then 11. Instead they are 11 and then 9.
With a gap of 9, the number after 17 should be 17 + 9 = 26. Then 26 + 11 = 37, which fits.
So the number that does not belong is 28.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The gaps should be 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, so the number after 17 should be 26, not 28.
misconceptions.B: 10 fits the pattern, because 5 + 5 = 10 and the gaps so far are 3 and then 5. Keep checking the gaps further along.
misconceptions.C: 37 fits once the pattern is put right, because the gaps 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 add up to 35 and 2 + 35 = 37. Look at the number just before it.
misconceptions.D: 17 fits the pattern, because 10 + 7 = 17 and the gaps so far are 3, 5, 7. The break comes after 17.

questionText: Find the next term: 4, 12, 36, 108, ______
hints: The numbers grow faster and faster, so adding the same amount will not fit. See what each term is multiplied by to get the next one.
Compare 4 and 12, then 12 and 36. Ask yourself how many times bigger each term is than the one before.
Here is a similar one: 2, 10, 50, 250. Each term is 5 times the one before. So the next term is 250 × 5 = 1250.

stepByStep.text: See how each term is made from the one before: 4 × 3 = 12, 12 × 3 = 36 and 36 × 3 = 108.
Each term is 3 times the one before. Multiply 108 by 3 to find that the next term is 324.

misconceptions.A: 144 is 108 + 36. This pattern multiplies each time, so multiply 108 by 3.
misconceptions.B: Great job! Each term is 3 times the one before, and 108 × 3 = 324.
misconceptions.C: 216 is 108 × 2. Check the earlier terms: 4 is multiplied by 3 to give 12, not by 2.
misconceptions.D: 432 is 108 × 4. Check the earlier terms: 4 is multiplied by 3 to give 12, not by 4.

questionText: The sequence 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, 42 follows the pattern n × (n+1). What is the 10th term?
hints: The rule is given to you: each term is its position number multiplied by the next counting number. You only need to use the rule for the right position.
Check the rule on a term you know. The 3rd term is 3 × 4 = 12. Now decide which two numbers to multiply for the 10th term.
Here is a similar one. With the same rule, the 7th term is 7 times the next counting number, which is 8. 7 × 8 = 56, so the 7th term is 56.

stepByStep.text: The rule says the term in position n is n times the number just after n. Check it: the 1st term is 1 × 2 = 2 and the 2nd term is 2 × 3 = 6.
For the 10th term, n is 10 and the number just after it is 11.
Multiply 10 by 11. The 10th term is 110.

misconceptions.A: Excellent thinking! The 10th term is 10 times the next number, 11, which is 110.
misconceptions.B: 90 is 9 × 10, which is the 9th term. For the 10th term, multiply 10 by the number after it.
misconceptions.C: 100 is 10 × 10. The rule multiplies 10 by the next number, which is 11.
misconceptions.D: 120 is 10 × 12. The rule uses the number just after 10, which is 11.

hints: The numbers get smaller quickly, so they are probably being divided rather than having something taken away. Look for the number that each one is divided by.
Divide a number by the one after it, for example 27 ÷ 9 or 81 ÷ 27. If you get the same result each time, that is the rule.
Here is a similar one: 400, 200, 100, 50, and then a blank. Each number is the one before it divided by 2, since 400 ÷ 2 = 200 and 200 ÷ 2 = 100. So the next number is 50 ÷ 2 = 25.

stepByStep.text: So each number is the one before it divided by 3.
Divide the last number by 3: 9 ÷ 3 = 3. The next number is 3.

misconceptions.A: 0 would come from taking 9 away from 9. In this pattern each number is divided by the same amount, so it never reaches 0.
misconceptions.B: 1 comes from dividing 9 by 9, or from taking two steps instead of one. Find what each number is divided by to get the next, and take just one step from 9.
misconceptions.C: 6 comes from 9 − 3. The numbers here do not go down by taking away. Check 27 ÷ 9 and 81 ÷ 27 to find the rule.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Each number is the one before it divided by 3, and 9 ÷ 3 = 3.

hints: This looks like two patterns woven together. Try reading every other number, and then the numbers in between.
Write down the 1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th and 9th numbers on one line. Write the 2nd, 4th, 6th and 8th numbers on another line and compare the two lines.
Here is a similar one: 1, 2, 2, 4, 3, 6, 4. The 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th numbers are 1, 2, 3 and 4. The number after each of them is its double: 2, 4, 6. So after the 4 comes its double, 8.

stepByStep.text: Two patterns are woven together. Take every other number, starting from the first: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. These are the counting numbers.
Now take the numbers in between: 1, 4, 9, 16. Each one is the number just before it multiplied by itself: 2 × 2 = 4, 3 × 3 = 9 and 4 × 4 = 16.
The gap comes straight after 5, so it is 5 multiplied by itself. The next term is 25.

misconceptions.A: 20 is 4 × 5. Each in-between number is the number before it multiplied by itself, so use 5 × 5.
misconceptions.B: You got it! Each in-between number is the number before it multiplied by itself, and 5 × 5 = 25.
misconceptions.C: 6 would carry on the counting numbers, but the gap belongs to the other pattern: 1, 4, 9, 16.
misconceptions.D: 10 is double 5. Look at the pairs 2 and 4, 3 and 9, 4 and 16 to see what is done to each number.
